In the coastal city of intoxication and revelry, night was the time for banquets. The city streets were alight with spectacle and song, bodies swaying in dances of drunken stupor. An unending feast; if not for the dawn that would bring morning over the horizon, so long as the black tide remained far from Styxia’s shores.

Day and night they remained vigilant for pollution in their waters. It was a war of attrition and the black tide was slowly gaining ground as every surge presented near endless waves of enemies to crash against the dwindling number of Phagousa’s Titankin. A siege in which the black tide launched unending ammunition from its catapults, whittling down defences, morale, and forcing them to crumble one assault at a time. 

Meanwhile, the sirens had to be cautious. There was no city walls to hide behind. One jab too eager could bring a corruption that couldn’t be recovered from even with Phagousa’s cleansing blessing. One dart in the wrong direction could have them swept into the depths of the black tide and never recovered. One moment of hesitation in front of a former comrade twisted by the black tide could spread that very infestation. 

It was a great responsibility, a burden as heavy upon the Ocean’s Titankin as Mydei. But, for now, it was safe to revel in the pleasures of peace through song and wine. 

Dusk sunk into night and Styxia’s place choked with the clink of chalices and laughter from those who emptied them.

After two months of monitoring the seabed, surfacing brought an ache to Mydei’s eyes and head from the differences in light and pressure between sea and land. Phagousa’s golden waters eased him through the pains of acclimatisation, splintering through the bones of his legs. It had been hours of rest since he split his tail. He would need to emerge from the siren baths soon. 

Tonight was a celebration. Not only of life and Phagousa’s blessings of plenty, but of military conquest. Styxia’s army had returned from their months long campaign against Corinth, spurred on by some territory disputes, leaving the soldiers zealous to shed the shackles of military discipline with debauchery. 

As Mydei dried his hair, his vocal cords naturally hummed along to the ebb and flow of the instruments rising through the palace’s floor and open windows. The beat of the tympanon, the blow of the aulos, and the strings of the kithara. In it he heard the sea currents carrying beguiling voices through the coral reefs. The sirens were leading the ensemble tonight. 

He fastened his chiton with a brooch spiralled like a shell and studded with pearls. He had no intention to dance on his aching feet so he donned a casual pair of loose sandals. 

It wasn’t Helektra at the concerto’s fore. If it were then he may have felt inclined to join them for a song or two. As the most skilled siren, beloved by Phagousa for her masterful drag of the bow as deadly as a sword, and the one destined to best the Coreflame of Ocean, her music called to all sirens. 

To join. To sing and play in harmony. To enliven the air as they had once done the water and return home, if only for a fleeting moment. Perhaps that was why it had been so long since Helektra last sang. 

His necklace rested against his breastbone, warmed with the heat of the baths. The bulk of his earring and necklace’s gold plates and blue jewels, too dark to harken back to the dazzling sea always so bright and lovely, were a stark contrast against the dainty silver and pearls adorned by Mydei’s comrades. 

But his jewellery and red markings deeper than skin were the only things that remained from the time before Phagousa’s blessing. They were too important to discard into the currents that would viciously tear apart something so foreign, even if he couldn’t articulate why. 

His hair had stopped dripping but wasn’t yet fully dry. Even if it were, he would have left it hand loose past his shoulder just the same. Someone had a habit of whining whenever he was deprived of the privilege to style Mydei’s hair with his own hands. 

Satisfied, Mydei left the siren baths. He would have preferred to retreat to his quarters with only a brief stop in the kitchen to cook something quick but filling enough to hold him over until morning. Even without the long distance covered through the day, his body was exhausted by the transition from a tail to two legs. 

But there was something he craved more than a warm meal, a cool towel draped over his eyes, and a soft mattress to sleep soundly upon. 

Someone that could only be found mingling amongst the musicians and the revellers. Stood between the two when he lacked the skill with a voice and instrument inherent to sirens, but too sober to carouse with the drunkards that would touch him with eager hands intent on snaring him in their bed, a wall or even a floor would suffice. 

Mydei couldn’t fault their zeal. Pretty white hair like sea foam blooming along the cusp of waves. Eyes like the tranquil sea on the calmest spring days. The sculpted body of a warrior still lithe with grace. A smile and voice that made even the most insignificant pleasure-seeker feel seen and important. It was difficult to believe only one of them was a siren.

The dimness may have masked his gills and scales but the sharp fins rising from where they had laid flat against his forearms were unmistakable when he crossed his arms. Combined with the pin on his chiton, they could harbour no doubts over who, or what, had laid claim to the target they were foolish enough to pick.

Mydei hummed, not too different from a lyre with a broken string in need of replacing go return to its usual fine notes. Some rest would be enough. “Done.” 

In the small space between them, Phainon’s hand fell atop Mydei’s palm. Not the usual confident grasp or playful tease up his palm and fingertips. The slip of their fingers together, Phainon’s hold loose where it was usually as strong as Mydei’s curling tight, was bashful. 

Phainon spent the whole night destroying Mydei’s back, pelvis and thighs along with their kline and now he was embarrassed. 

“I considered something,” Phainon annunciated slowly, preplanned words like a commander giving his first speech to his new soldiers. Mydei withheld a snarky comment while he waited for Phainon to continue. “The pearls are a gift from you.” 

A gift. Sure. Ones Phainon extorted from his body with the possessed fervour of a madman. 

“I can’t—I can’t make anything like… that,” Phainon stammered clumsily and his face flushed again, not from passion nor exertion but sheer humiliation. “But I could… there are still things I can give you.” 

Mydei blinked languidly but Phainon was too preoccupied staring at their hands to notice that Mydei was waiting for him to continue. 

He squeezed Phainon’s hand, as reassuring as his drained body could manage. “Whatever you give me—it will be mine to keep. None can take it from me, not even you.” 

An encouragement spoken from the depths of Mydei’s heart, deeper than the sea trenches and filled to the roiling surface with Mydei’s love. And calmed by a doting but ravenous affection that crashed against it only to meld perfectly, as though they were born from the same source and intended to meet and mingle into one, remaining as such, before the final end. 

Phainon breathed deep, bracing himself as he lifted their hands and turned them so Mydei’s was overtop, making it easy to bring  his hand, one finger in particular, to Phainon’s lips. 

The warmth lingered even as Phainon tilted his head back to peer up and quietly, just for the two of them to hear, declared,  “A ring forged for your hand alone.” 

To exchange rings was a human tradition. Mydei had lived as a siren longer than a human, and it showed in his greediest instincts. Protective of everything Phainon was willing to give him. So his heart quickened and his vocal cords vibrated with the beginnings of a pleased noise. 

“That’s what it meant. Back then,” Phainon said, unsure despite the bravado he shoved into his voice. “When you gave me the scale from the tip of your heart.” 

Sirens exchanged plenty of things apart from rings. Music compositions, lyrics, food. Most notable was scales. After all, every siren’s was unique. To give a scale from the heart was to say: I want you. I want to be connected to you. I want us to be more than friends or fall into mere strangers. It was a request, an offering, a trade to be family. 

It wasn’t overtly romantic either—if Mydei had plucked any scale from over his chest. But to give a scale from the tip of his heart meant to hand over the cleanest, purest part of his heart and his love. 

Back then he was less certain, too young and inexperienced to articulate what he wanted. He only knew he wanted Phainon to stay. Now he knew better. 

Mydei turned over their hands so he could lift Phainon’s fourth finger to his lips, leaving a kiss just as tender as the one given to him. “Don’t forget to forge one for yourself.” 

Phainon’s lips split around a grin, as dazzling as the rising sun scattered across the hills and valleys of the sea. 

“Not a single pearl,” Mydei commanded and Phainon nodded eagerly. Especially not the pearls on the kline. “Something blue would be more fitting.”

“Oh! To match your other jewellery,” Phainon said and fiddled with Mydei’s finger as though he could already see the ring there. 

Mydei clicked his tongue. “No.”

He tilted his head, hair ruffling against the pillow, with pure confusion in the crease of his brow. How dare he act cute when Mydei was still sore everywhere because of him. 

Mydei bit the swell of his cheek and Phainon yelped but it was more surprised than displeased. He even pouted, wide eyed, as he rubbed at ring of teeth marks left behind. 

But Mydei ignored him, closing his eyes. “Use your brain. I’m going to sleep.” 

Phainon laughed and Mydei kept his body lax as the mattress shifted with Phainon’s shuffle closer. His warm body pressed against Mydei and he trapped the heat in with the pull of a blanket over them. 

His hand rested against Mydei’s thigh, tracing skin rather than scales. “Sleep well.” 

There was only one blue Mydei wanted to wear. Not the green-blue of the sea nor the dark blue of jewellery chained to a past. It had to be the open skies, taken from a perfect spring day that stretched over the sea and the wheat fields. 

He peeked an eye open. Phainon was already asleep, mouth slack around slow, deep breaths. Mydei snuck a kiss against each of his eyelids. He was eager to see the gift Phainon prepared for him, and how pretty Phainon would look draped in his pearls.
